$comment: Content for Many Ways to Family (node g60, ages 22+, Chapter 7): NEW v2 build to GDD 60 (mechanic-embodying),
the EQUITY NODE CLOSING Chapter 7 and the counterpart to If, When & Whether (g59): for everyone whose route to
parenthood isn't the default biological one. 84 researched, India-grounded scenarios across every-route-real →
the-routes → the-real-path → name-the-barriers → your-family-your-way → tools-and-help, each encoded as one of
the shared v2 play actions (strike-rewrite / match / sort / reflect / branch / role-play / spot): no binary
"tap the right card". Lead: strike-rewrite (bust the myth), match, sort. Six modes: every route is real family
(busts "real family is only biological"; adoptive, single, queer, blended and childfree families are fully
real), the routes (what adoption, fostering, IVF/ART, surrogacy, single & LGBTQ+ parenthood each involve, with
the right official first step), the real path (honest steps, timelines, costs & emotions; no romanticising and
no false hope; setbacks aren't a verdict), name the barriers (India's specific, gendered & legal barriers told
honestly so people aren't blindsided), your family your way (dignity, chosen family, support, family acceptance
on your terms), tools & help (the routes/eligibility reference, CARA & licensed clinics, current dated legal
info). LEGAL/ELIGIBILITY content is GENERAL, DATED (researched 2024-25) and EVOLVING (NOT legal advice) and
must be verified and localised: under CARA (2022) a single man may adopt a boy but not a girl while a single
woman may adopt any gender; the Surrogacy & ART Acts (2021) are altruistic-only and mainly for married couples;
and since Supriyo v. Union of India (Oct 2023) same-sex marriage is not legally recognised in India, so same-sex
couples cannot marry or jointly adopt, though a single LGBTQ+ person can adopt as a single applicant. Every
family form is treated with full dignity, none framed as lesser; LGBTQ+ content handled with the care of
Spectrum (no outing). Builds on Spectrum (g32) and Your Path, Your Call (g54). India: CARA single-man
girl-child rule, surrogacy/ART restrictions, no same-sex marriage or joint adoption, single-mother stigma;
official routes via CARA and licensed ART clinics. gameId "many-ways-to-family".
title: Many Ways to Family
greet: Hey, it’s Lensy. Family comes in many real shapes: adoptive, single, queer, blended, childfree. We’ll walk the honest routes, so nothing blindsides you.

badge.title: Many Ways to Family 👪
badge.blurb: You know real family is never only biological: adoptive, single, queer, blended and childfree are all real, and a setback isn’t a verdict. Your way. 💛

helpLine: Every family is real. Routes: adoption & fostering via CARA, IVF/ART/surrogacy via clinics. Laws evolve, not legal advice; verify with NALSA 15100.
reassure: Every route to family is real, and so is yours. A setback is never a verdict on your worth. Support exists: CARA, clinics, NALSA legal aid 15100. 💛

scenarios.hook: "Real family is only the one you make biologically."

myth.un: Real family is only the one you make biologically.
myth.re: Family is built in many ways, and a family built by adoption, ART, blending or choice is fully real.
myth.why: Family is defined by love and commitment, not biology alone.

scenarios.relearn: Family is built in many ways; adoptive, blended and chosen families are fully real.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a real, valid family, or 'not a real family' the way prejudice frames it?
scenarios.relearn: Adoptive, single-parent and childfree families are real; 'lesser', 'doesn't count', 'playing' are prejudice.

scenarios.hook: "A child needs a 'normal' mother-and-father home or they'll be damaged."

myth.un: A child needs a 'normal' mother-and-father home or they'll be damaged.
myth.re: What children need most is stable, loving care, which many family forms provide well.
myth.why: Love and stability matter far more than family shape.

scenarios.relearn: Children thrive on stable, loving care, which many family forms provide; one shape isn't required.

scenarios.hook: Match each family form to the truth about it.

pairs.right: Bonded by love and law, fully real
Complete and capable on its own
A real family, whatever the law lags
A whole family of two by choice

scenarios.relearn: Adoptive, single-parent, LGBTQ+, blended and childfree families are each fully real, whatever stigma says.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: there isn't one right shape for a family, only loving, stable ones in many forms. Sit right?
scenarios.affirm: There is no single right family shape; what matters is love and stability, found in many forms.
scenarios.relearn: There's no one right family shape, only loving, stable ones in many forms.

scenarios.hook: "Choosing not to have children means you'll never have a real family."

myth.un: Choosing not to have children means you'll never have a real family.
myth.re: A childfree life can be rich with family, partners, chosen family and deep bonds are family too.
myth.why: Family isn't only parents and children.

scenarios.relearn: A childfree life can be full of family; partners and chosen family are real family too.

scenarios.hook: Spot the 2 lines that don't belong (the red flags) about what makes a family; the other 3 are true.

scene.text: Love, care and commitment
A specific biological link
Showing up for each other over time
Everyone sharing the same surname by birth
Choosing each other and staying

scenarios.why: A specific biological link and a shared birth-surname aren't what make a family; love and showing up are.
scenarios.relearn: Family is made by love, care and showing up, not by a biological link or a shared birth-surname.

scenarios.hook: At a family mehendi, an aunt tells you and your partner Dev your adopted son isn't really family.

steps.prompt: She waits for a reaction. What do you say?

options.text: Say he's fully your son, made by love and care
options.then: The aunt pauses, surprised, and doesn't push it further tonight.

options.text: Change the subject to keep the evening light
options.then: The evening stays smooth, but her words go unanswered.

options.text: Snap at her loudly in front of the whole hall
options.then: Heads turn, and the moment becomes about your anger, not hers.

options.text: Ask Dev to handle it instead of answering
options.then: Dev answers kindly, but her words still sit with you.

steps.why: Naming your family as real, calmly, closes the doubt without a scene.

steps.prompt: A week later, your mother calls to say relatives are still discussing the comment. What do you do?

options.text: Tell her the matter is settled, nothing to discuss
options.then: She goes quiet, then says she will pass that along.

options.text: Ask her to smooth it over with the aunt herself
options.then: She agrees, but the fix now depends on someone else speaking for you.

options.text: Offer to explain your choices to the whole family
options.then: You spend an hour defending a decision that never needed it.

options.text: Say the relatives can talk it out among themselves
options.then: She isn't sure who's meant to respond, and the gossip carries on.

steps.why: Telling family the matter is settled protects your peace, not theirs.

steps.prompt: At the next gathering, your son asks why the aunt looked at him strangely. What do you tell him?

options.text: Say some people don't understand family, but he's loved
options.then: He nods, reassured, and goes back to the sweets table.

options.text: Say nothing happened, so he doesn't worry about it
options.then: He drops it, but the odd look stays unexplained in his mind.

options.text: Say that aunt is simply a bad person to avoid
options.then: He looks unsettled, unsure why an elder is suddenly bad.

options.text: Tell him to go ask Dev about it later tonight
options.then: He waits, and the moment for a simple answer passes.

steps.why: A simple warm answer keeps your child secure instead of confused.

scenarios.debrief: Your family is real and built on love; you can affirm that calmly against doubt.
scenarios.relearn: Affirm your family's reality calmly; prejudice doesn't get to define your home.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: every route here, adoption, ART, solo, queer, blended, childfree, builds something real. Land okay?
scenarios.affirm: Adoption, ART, solo, queer, blended and childfree paths all build something real and worthy.
scenarios.relearn: Every route, adoption, ART, solo, queer, blended, childfree, builds a real family.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a dignity-affirming view of family, or a ranking that shouldn't exist?

items.text: All family forms are equally valid

scenarios.relearn: All forms equally valid and respected is dignity; ranking biological or others above is a false hierarchy.

scenarios.hook: "Adopted children are somehow less 'your own' than biological ones."

myth.un: Adopted children are somehow less 'your own' than biological ones.
myth.re: Adopted children are fully and truly your own; parenthood is built through love and care, not just genes.
myth.why: Bonding makes a parent, not biology.

scenarios.relearn: Adopted children are fully your own; parenthood is built through love and care, not genes alone.

scenarios.hook: Match each myth about non-default families to the dignified truth.

pairs.right: Loving, stable care is what helps kids
Adopted children are fully their own
Partners and chosen people are family

scenarios.relearn: Each myth about non-default families has a dignified, evidence-aligned truth that replaces it.

scenarios.hook: Match each route to family to what it broadly involves.

pairs.right: Becoming the legal parent of a child who needs a family
Caring for a child for a time, not always permanently
Another person carries a pregnancy for intended parents
Building a family on your own, by choice or path

scenarios.relearn: Adoption, fostering, IVF/ART, surrogacy and single parenthood are distinct routes, each with its own process and purpose.

scenarios.hook: Match each further route to what it broadly involves.

pairs.right: Two families joining, often with step-children
A surrogate carries without commercial payment
A relative raises a child who needs a home
Two adults raising a child without being a couple
A single applicant adopting on their own

scenarios.relearn: Blended families, altruistic surrogacy, kinship care, co-parenting and solo adoption are all real, distinct routes to family.

scenarios.hook: "Adoption is a quick, simple way to instantly get a child."

myth.un: Adoption is a quick, simple way to instantly get a child.
myth.re: Adoption is a meaningful legal process with assessment, waiting and preparation; it's worth it but not instant.
myth.why: Knowing the real process helps you prepare.

scenarios.relearn: Adoption is a meaningful legal process with assessment and waiting, not an instant or simple shortcut.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a route to becoming a parent, or something else entirely?

items.text: Adopting a child who needs a family

scenarios.relearn: Adoption, ART and fostering are routes to parenthood; a wedding, a house and a holiday are not, in themselves.

scenarios.hook: You're drawn to building a family but unsure which route actually fits your life.

steps.prompt: You start researching one evening. What do you focus on first?

options.text: What each route actually involves, step by step
options.then: You start to see how different adoption, fostering and ART really are.

options.text: Which route sounds the most impressive to say out loud
options.then: A route that sounds good out loud starts to pull ahead in your head.

options.text: Whatever your friends happened to choose
options.then: You bookmark the route two friends took, without checking it against your life.

options.text: Nothing yet, since it all feels overwhelming
options.then: The overwhelm keeps you from learning even the basics.

steps.why: Understanding each route's real shape lets you choose from knowledge, not guesswork.

steps.prompt: A week in, a friend asks which route you're leaning toward. What do you tell her?

options.text: Honestly, that you haven't decided yet
options.then: She nods, and asks what's still unclear.

options.text: Whatever sounds most decided, to seem further along
options.then: The false certainty makes it harder to admit you're still deciding.

options.text: That you'll probably just pick adoption. It's simplest
options.then: You haven't actually checked if that's true yet.

options.text: That you'd rather not talk about it until it's settled
options.then: She stops asking, and you lose a sounding board.

steps.why: Naming that you're still deciding, honestly, keeps the choice open to real information.

steps.prompt: You narrow it down to two routes that could both work. What tips the choice?

options.text: Which one genuinely fits your life right now
options.then: The choice feels solid, because it's actually yours.

options.text: Which one your family would approve of more
options.then: The route fits their comfort more than your actual life.

options.text: Whichever seems faster on paper
options.then: Speed alone leaves out whether it truly fits you.

options.text: Flip a coin, since both seem fine
options.then: You commit to a route without really choosing it.

steps.why: Choosing on genuine fit, not approval or speed, keeps the decision truly yours.

scenarios.debrief: Understand what each route really involves before choosing the one that fits your life.
scenarios.relearn: Learn each route honestly first; choose the fit from understanding, not a vague impression.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: knowing the map of routes, adoption, fostering, ART, surrogacy, solo, blended, is power. Useful?
scenarios.affirm: Knowing the full map of routes to family lets you choose the one that fits, with eyes open.
scenarios.relearn: Knowing the map of routes, adoption, fostering, ART, surrogacy, solo, blended, is empowering.

scenarios.hook: Match a starting point to a sensible first step.

pairs.right: Learn the CARA process and register
Find an authorised agency to ask

scenarios.relearn: Each route has a sensible, official first step: CARA, a licensed clinic, an authorised agency, or NALSA 15100 for rights.

scenarios.hook: "Fostering and adoption are the same thing."

myth.un: Fostering and adoption are the same thing.
myth.re: Fostering is caring for a child for a time, often not permanent; adoption makes you the child's legal parent.
myth.why: They're different commitments with different aims.

scenarios.relearn: Fostering is temporary care; adoption makes you the legal parent, they're different routes.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two unrealistic expectations about a route to family.

scene.text: There's a process and a wait
It happens instantly with no steps
Support and guidance are available
Every route is guaranteed to succeed
Eligibility rules differ by route

scenarios.why: Instant-with-no-steps and a guarantee are unrealistic; a process, a wait, support and route-specific rules are the real picture.
scenarios.relearn: Routes involve a process, a wait, support and route-specific rules, not instant or guaranteed results.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: there's a route for many different lives here, and a real first step for each. Reassuring?
scenarios.affirm: Whatever your life looks like, there is likely a route to family here, each with a real first step.
scenarios.relearn: There's a route to family for many lives, each with a real, doable first step.

scenarios.hook: "These routes are easy and emotion-free if you just want it enough."

myth.un: These routes are easy and emotion-free if you just want it enough.
myth.re: Routes like adoption and ART have real steps, costs, waits and big emotions; honesty helps you prepare and cope.
myth.why: Knowing the real path beats a fantasy of it.

scenarios.relearn: Routes like adoption and ART carry real steps, costs and emotions; honesty helps you prepare and cope.

scenarios.hook: Sort: a realistic part of these journeys, or a false promise to distrust?

items.text: No costs and no setbacks ever
Honest odds from a licensed clinic
A baby handed over with no process

scenarios.relearn: Waits, paperwork, emotions and honest odds are realistic; guaranteed success, zero cost and a no-process baby are false promises.

scenarios.hook: You're starting a family-building journey and expecting it to be smooth and fast.

steps.prompt: You sit down to make a plan with your partner. What do you do first?

options.text: Set realistic expectations together, and line up support
options.then: You both feel steadier, ready for the ups and downs ahead.

options.text: Pick the option that sounds fastest, and start right away
options.then: You start quickly, unprepared for the delays that follow.

options.text: Assume the worst and prepare for total failure
options.then: The worst-case planning leaves you anxious before you've even started.

options.text: Avoid planning for now, and deal with it as it comes
options.then: The lack of a plan leaves you scrambling at the first setback.

steps.why: Realistic expectations and support build the resilience this journey needs.

steps.prompt: A month in, the paperwork takes far longer than either of you expected. What do you do?

options.text: Remind each other this is a normal part of the process
options.then: You both stay steady, expecting the wait rather than fighting it.

options.text: Assume something's gone wrong with your application
options.then: The worry builds over a delay that's actually completely normal.

options.text: Call the office daily, demanding faster updates
options.then: The office notes the calls, but the pace doesn't actually change.

options.text: Stop checking in on it, to avoid the frustration
options.then: You lose track of where things stand, and miss a needed step.

steps.why: Naming the wait as normal keeps you steady instead of alarmed.

steps.prompt: A friend who tried a similar route says it never worked out for them. What do you do?

options.text: Listen to their story, and still line up your own support
options.then: You hold their story and your own hope, both at once.

options.text: Take their story as proof it won't work for you either
options.then: Doubt creeps in, right when you need to stay steady.

options.text: Tell them their experience surely won't happen to you
options.then: Your friend feels dismissed, and the friendship feels strained.

options.text: Avoid the friend, since their story feels discouraging
options.then: You lose a source of real, lived experience by pulling away.

steps.why: Holding someone else's outcome without adopting it as your own keeps you steady.

steps.prompt: Six months in, the journey is harder than you imagined. What do you do?

options.text: Lean on whatever support you can find, at your own pace
options.then: The support carries you through the hardest stretch so far.

options.text: Push through completely alone, without telling anyone
options.then: The weight builds, unshared, until it feels heavier than it needs to.

options.text: Decide the whole journey was a mistake from the start
options.then: The setback gets read as a verdict, instead of a normal hard stretch.

options.text: Switch to another route in a panic, to escape the strain
options.then: The new route has its own waits, and the strain simply moves with you.

steps.why: Leaning on support through the hard stretch is what makes it survivable.

scenarios.debrief: Set realistic expectations and support for a family-building journey; it has ups and downs.
scenarios.relearn: Expect ups and downs and line up support, not a smooth ride.

scenarios.hook: Match each part of the real path to how to meet it.

pairs.right: Patience and support to hold steady
Lean on partner, friends or counselling
Follow the official steps in order

scenarios.relearn: The waiting, costs, emotions, paperwork and setbacks of these routes are each met with planning and support.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: honest about the hard parts isn't discouraging, it's what lets you go in strong. Agree?
scenarios.affirm: Honesty about the hard parts of a route isn't discouragement; it's preparation that builds strength.
scenarios.relearn: Honesty about the hard parts prepares you to go in strong, it isn't discouragement.

scenarios.hook: "If a route is hard or has setbacks, it means it wasn't 'meant to be'."

myth.un: If a route is hard or has setbacks, it means it wasn't 'meant to be'.
myth.re: Difficulty is normal on these paths and isn't a verdict; setbacks can be part of a journey that still works out.
myth.why: Hard doesn't mean wrong.

scenarios.relearn: Difficulty and setbacks are normal on these routes and aren't a verdict that it wasn't meant to be.

scenarios.hook: Spot the two unhealthy ways of handling a setback on the path.

scene.text: Grieve it, get support, reassess calmly
Take it as proof you don't deserve family
Ask what the next honest option is
Decide it means family wasn't meant to be
Let yourself feel it, then keep going

scenarios.why: 'I don't deserve family' and 'it wasn't meant to be' are unhealthy ways of reading a normal setback. Catch them.
scenarios.relearn: Meet setbacks with grief, support and the next honest option, not self-blame or a false verdict.

scenarios.hook: A route's costs and waits are heavier than you expected, and you feel discouraged.

steps.prompt: You sit with the numbers late one night. What do you do?

options.text: Reassess your options honestly, with your partner and support
options.then: Together, you start looking at routes that might fit better.

options.text: Push forward on the same route, no matter the cost
options.then: The strain builds, and the same heavy costs keep piling up.

options.text: Decide family isn't possible for people like you
options.then: The conclusion closes a door that was actually still open.

options.text: Avoid the numbers for now, and revisit them later
options.then: The numbers wait, unchanged, for a later that keeps slipping.

steps.why: Reassessing honestly, with support, keeps family possible another way.

steps.prompt: Your partner suggests looking into adoption as well as the original route. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're open to exploring it properly together
options.then: You both start researching adoption with real curiosity.

options.text: Say it feels like giving up on the original plan
options.then: The idea sits there, half considered, half dismissed.

options.text: Say you'd rather decide alone, without discussing it together
options.then: The conversation ends there, and your partner is left in the dark.

options.text: Say you'll think about it, without really deciding
options.then: The suggestion quietly drops, without either of you deciding.

steps.why: Staying open to another route keeps more doors available to you.

steps.prompt: A relative says you should have picked the cheaper route from the start. What do you do?

options.text: Explain you're handling this thoughtfully, with the facts you have
options.then: The relative nods, hearing the reasoning behind your approach.

options.text: Agree, and feel worse about the choices you've made
options.then: The self-doubt grows, right when you need steadiness most.

options.text: Tell the relative to stay out of your finances
options.then: The relative backs off, but the relationship feels strained.

options.text: Change the subject to avoid the comment entirely
options.then: The comment goes unanswered, and might return again later.

steps.why: Explaining your reasoning holds your ground without inviting more doubt.

steps.prompt: Months later, the route starts moving forward steadily. What do you do?

options.text: Notice the progress, and keep leaning on your support
options.then: You feel steadier, trusting the process you're in.

options.text: Assume the hard part is entirely over now
options.then: A later bump catches you off guard, unprepared again.

options.text: Dwell on the time and money already spent
options.then: The dwelling takes up energy the actual process needs.

options.text: Stay braced for the worst, even as things go well
options.then: The bracing keeps you from noticing real, steady progress.

steps.why: Noticing progress while still leaning on support keeps you grounded.

scenarios.debrief: If one route is too heavy, reassess options with support; family may be possible another way.
scenarios.relearn: Reassess routes with support if one's too heavy; don't write off family.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: many families took a hard, winding road to exist, and they're no less joyful for it. Comforting?
scenarios.affirm: Many families came through hard, winding paths and are no less real or joyful for the journey.
scenarios.relearn: Many families took a hard road to exist and are no less joyful for it.

scenarios.hook: "The rules for building a family are the same for everyone in India."

myth.un: The rules for building a family are the same for everyone in India.
myth.re: Access is unequal: some routes are gendered and restricted by law, so it helps to know the barriers before you start.
myth.why: Knowing the barriers means you go in informed.

scenarios.relearn: Access to family-building in India is unequal and partly gendered by law; knowing the barriers helps you prepare.

scenarios.hook: Sort: who can adopt a girl child under India's CARA 2022 rules?

items.text: A single woman over 45 (within age bands)
A married couple in a stable two-year marriage

scenarios.relearn: Under CARA 2022 a married couple and a single woman can adopt a girl child; a single man cannot, a gendered rule.

scenarios.hook: "A single man being barred from adopting a girl is just sensible caution."

myth.un: A single man being barred from adopting a girl is just sensible caution.
myth.re: Under CARA 2022 a single man may adopt a boy but not a girl, a real gendered barrier worth naming, even where caution is the stated aim.
myth.why: Name the barrier honestly, whatever its rationale.

scenarios.relearn: CARA 2022 lets a single man adopt a boy but not a girl, a gendered barrier worth naming honestly.

scenarios.hook: Match each India law to what it currently means (2024-25, evolving).

pairs.right: Singles can adopt; single men only boys
A door open to a single LGBTQ+ person

scenarios.relearn: CARA, the Surrogacy and ART Acts, the marriage ruling and single-applicant adoption each shape who can access which route; the law evolves.

scenarios.hook: "Because same-sex marriage isn't recognised, queer people can't build any family in India."

myth.un: Because same-sex marriage isn't recognised, queer people can't build any family in India.
myth.re: Same-sex couples can't currently marry or jointly adopt in India, but a single LGBTQ+ person can adopt as a single applicant, and chosen family is real.
myth.why: Barriers are real, and so are the open doors.

scenarios.relearn: Same-sex couples can't marry or jointly adopt in India, but a single LGBTQ+ person can, and chosen family is real.

scenarios.hook: Sort: an accurate statement of India's current rules, or a misconception?

items.text: Single women can adopt any gender
Single men can adopt a girl child
A single LGBTQ+ person can adopt alone
The rules are identical for everyone

scenarios.relearn: Single women adopting any gender, altruistic-only surrogacy and single-applicant LGBTQ+ adoption are accurate; the rest are myths.

scenarios.hook: Lensy: naming a barrier isn't accepting it's fair, it's refusing to let it blindside you. Make sense?
scenarios.affirm: Naming a legal or gendered barrier is about going in informed, not endorsing it as fair.
scenarios.relearn: Naming a barrier is going in informed, not calling it fair.

scenarios.hook: You're told outright that people like you can't have a family in India.

steps.prompt: A friend says it flatly at dinner. What do you do?

options.text: Look up the actual current rules and the doors open to you
options.then: You find single men can adopt, though only boys, while joint adoption stays shut.

options.text: Believe him, and quietly give up on the whole idea
options.then: The idea of family quietly closes in your mind that night.

options.text: Argue with him for an hour without checking anything
options.then: You're both frustrated, and neither of you actually knows the rules.

options.text: Change the subject, since it feels too upsetting to discuss
options.then: The dinner moves on, but the fear stays unexamined.

steps.why: Checking the actual rules finds doors a blanket no was hiding.

steps.prompt: A week later, the topic comes up again with your partner. What do you say?

options.text: Suggest you both read CARA's current rules together
options.then: He agrees, and that weekend you go through the rules and their limits.

options.text: Say it's basically hopeless, like everyone always says
options.then: He nods, and the two of you drop the idea for now.

options.text: Say singles can adopt, so there's nothing to worry about
options.then: He relaxes, though neither of you knows the limits that apply.

options.text: Say the whole legal system is stacked against you both
options.then: He looks overwhelmed by how hopeless you've made it sound.

steps.why: Reading the current rules together gives you both facts, limits included, not a blanket no.

steps.prompt: At a family dinner, a cousin repeats that gay men can't have families here. What do you do?

options.text: Calmly say it's not that simple, and point him to CARA
options.then: The cousin looks surprised, and asks a genuine follow up question.

options.text: Let it go, since arguing with him never really works
options.then: The wrong idea stays in the room, unchallenged, for everyone.

options.text: Mock him for being so behind the times, honestly
options.then: The cousin gets defensive and the table turns tense.

options.text: Ask your partner to correct him instead of you
options.then: Your partner corrects him, but the moment passes you by.

steps.why: Calmly questioning a blanket no, and naming the official source, spreads real facts further.

scenarios.debrief: Get the actual current rules; a blanket "people like you can't" usually hides open doors.
scenarios.relearn: Find the real rules and open doors; don't accept a blanket "people like you can't."

scenarios.hook: Spot the two barriers that are legal/structural, not just stigma to resist.

Relatives disapproving of a single mother

Neighbours gossiping about an adopted child
A colleague calling a childfree choice 'sad'

scenarios.relearn: Some barriers are legal/structural and some are stigma; telling them apart shapes how you respond.

scenarios.hook: Your partner is discouraged after a setback in the adoption process.

steps.prompt: She says: "Maybe this is a sign we should just stop."

options.text: "This is a hard step, not the end. Let's plan the next move together."

options.text: "You might be right. Maybe we should just drop it for good."

options.text: "Don't be dramatic. It's only a setback. Everyone has them."
options.then: She looks stung. "I'm not being dramatic."

options.text: "I really don't want to talk about this right now, sorry."
options.then: She nods, then can't help but ask anyway, still worried.

steps.why: Naming it a step, not the end, keeps you moving as a team.

steps.prompt: She asks: "What if the next update is bad news too?"

options.text: "Then we'll face it together, and ask others who've done this."
options.then: She relaxes slightly. "Together. And maybe someone who's been there. Okay."

options.text: "Then I suppose that's how we'll know it was never meant to be."
options.then: She looks more discouraged, not less.

options.text: "It won't be. Please don't even think like that, not tonight."
options.then: "You don't actually know that," she says quietly.

options.text: "Let's cross that bridge when we get to it, not before then."
options.then: She nods, but the worry stays unanswered underneath.

steps.why: Facing bad news together, with others to lean on, steadies the fear behind her question.

steps.prompt: A week later, the update comes through, and it's good. She asks: "Does this mean the hard part's over?"

options.text: "Yes, totally, the worst is behind us now."
options.then: She relaxes completely, unprepared for whatever comes next.

options.text: "Who knows. Let's not jinx it."
options.then: The good news shrinks under the worry you just added.

options.text: "I honestly don't want to think about what comes after this one."
options.then: She's left holding the question alone, right after good news.

steps.why: Naming more steps ahead, honestly, keeps you both realistically hopeful.

scenarios.relearn: Naming a setback as a step, not the end, and reaching for support keeps you both moving as a team.

options.text: "You have no idea what this actually involves."

options.text: "Sure, I'll try to relax more."

options.text: "You wouldn't get it. It's complicated."

options.text: "I'd rather not get into it right now."

options.then: The advice stays a coin toss instead of something useful.

scenarios.hook: A young queer relative comes to you upset after something they read online.
scenarios.setup: They sit across from you at the kitchen table.

steps.prompt: They say: "So I guess family's just not happening for me, ever."

options.text: "Same-sex couples can't marry or adopt jointly, but you can adopt as a single."
options.then: They sit up a little. "Wait, really? I didn't know that."

options.text: "Yeah, sadly that's just true, no family for people like us."
options.then: They nod, sadly, taking the hopelessness as settled fact.

options.text: "Don't worry. The law will sort itself out soon enough."
options.then: They look skeptical. "You don't actually know that, though."

options.text: "Let's not talk about something so upsetting right now."
options.then: They pause. "I kind of need to talk about it, though."

steps.why: Naming both the real bar and the real door gives honest, grounded hope.

steps.prompt: They ask: "And if I have a partner someday, could we both be parents?"

options.text: "Not jointly, for now. One of you might apply as a single. Check CARA."
options.then: They exhale. "So not both of us, but not nothing either."

options.text: "Sure. One of you adopts, and then you're both legal parents."
options.then: They light up, not knowing only one of them would be the legal parent.

options.text: "Then honestly, that part might never really work for people like us."
options.then: They go quiet, and whatever hope they had fades.

options.text: "That's a bit far off to think about right now, isn't it?"
options.then: They're left with the same worry, just unspoken now.

steps.why: Being honest that it isn't joint, while naming the single route to check, keeps hope real.

options.text: "Just ask around. Someone will probably know."
options.then: They get mixed answers, and the confusion just continues.

options.text: "Honestly, I wouldn't bother looking into it yet."
options.then: They drop the question, discouraged before they've even started.

options.text: "I'll look into it for you and let you know."
options.then: They wait on you, instead of learning it for themselves.

steps.why: Pointing them to the official source builds their own grounded hope.

scenarios.relearn: Honest-with-hope names the real bar and the open door, instead of a crushing, untrue blanket never.

scenarios.hook: At a gathering, someone interrogates your choice to raise your child alone.

steps.prompt: They ask: "But don't you think a child needs two parents?"

options.text: "I chose this with care; my child is loved and thriving."

options.text: "I know, I know. It's not ideal."
options.then: They take that as agreement and keep pressing.

options.text: "Plenty of children do wonderfully with one parent, honestly."
options.then: They tilt their head. "Sure, but what about yours?"

options.text: "That's a rude thing to ask."
options.then: They blink, then repeat the question anyway.

steps.prompt: They try again: "Aren't you worried about what people will say?"

options.text: "I'm at peace with it, and that's enough."
options.then: They nod slowly. "Okay, fair enough."

options.text: "A bit. Maybe they're not entirely wrong."
options.then: They nod, encouraged. "See, that's what I mean."

options.text: "People can say whatever they like to say."
options.then: They raise an eyebrow. "You sound tired of the question, not settled."

options.text: "I try not to think about it."
options.then: They tilt their head. "That sounds like avoiding it, not peace."

steps.why: Naming your own peace with it, plainly, ends the question without sounding rattled.

steps.prompt: They finally say: "Well, I hope it works out for you."

options.text: "It already has. We're doing well."

options.text: "Thanks, I hope so too."
options.then: It leaves a little doubt in the air that didn't need to be there.

options.text: "We'll see, I guess."
options.then: It hands them the uncertainty they were hoping to find.

options.text: "I don't need your hope, honestly."
options.then: It's sharp, and it turns a closing moment into a small edge.

steps.why: Naming that it's already working closes the conversation on your own settled terms.

options.text: "That's a silly thing to wonder."

options.text: "Real enough. Don't overthink it."
options.then: It answers, but a little dismissively, and they notice.

steps.why: A clear, unhedged yes settles the question instead of leaving a little doubt in it.

steps.prompt: A few days later, they come home and say: "A friend at school asked me the same thing. What should I tell them?"

options.text: "Just say it's complicated and leave it there."

options.text: "You don't have to explain anything to anyone."

options.text: "Tell them it's none of their business."

scenarios.hook: The clinic explains your ART odds honestly, and they're sobering.

options.text: Look for a clinic that promises certain success

options.text: Decide the honest odds mean it's already hopeless

options.text: Avoid thinking about it until the next appointment

steps.prompt: Your partner asks what you actually think the odds mean for you both. What do you say?

options.text: That you'd rather focus on anything except the numbers

options.text: That the clinic is probably wrong or overcautious
options.then: He looks uneasy, unsure whether to trust the clinic's numbers now.

steps.prompt: A friend hears the odds and says you should switch to a clinic that guarantees success. What do you do?

options.text: Explain gently that no honest clinic can guarantee that

options.text: Consider switching, since a guarantee sounds better

options.text: Get defensive about your current clinic's numbers

options.text: Say nothing and let her keep believing the guarantee exists

steps.why: Naming that no clinic can guarantee success protects you from an empty promise.

scenarios.debrief: Honest odds let you plan and decide; a clinic promising certain success is a red flag.

scenarios.hook: Doubt creeps in mid journey: maybe you're not strong enough for this.

steps.prompt: The thought lands hardest late at night. What do you do with it?

options.text: Name it out loud to yourself instead of pushing it down
options.then: Saying it plainly makes it feel a little smaller by morning.

options.text: Treat it as proof you should just quit
options.then: You tell yourself it's decided, and stop looking for another way through.

options.text: Hide it and act like you feel nothing
options.then: Suppressing it makes it heavier by the next quiet night.

options.text: Scroll your phone until you're too tired to think
options.then: The doubt is still there, waiting, when the screen goes dark.

steps.why: Naming the doubt plainly keeps it from growing bigger in the dark.

steps.prompt: The next morning, your husband asks if something's on your mind. What do you tell him?

options.text: The honest doubt from last night, without softening it
options.then: He listens, and says he's had the same thought some nights.

options.text: That you're fine, just tired
options.then: He believes it, and the doubt stays yours to carry alone.

options.text: That the whole route was probably a mistake
options.then: He hears a decision, not the doubt that's actually underneath it.

options.text: Nothing, since he can't really help anyway
options.then: You decide for him that he can't help, without asking.

steps.why: Telling him the honest doubt lets him actually stand with you in it.

steps.prompt: At a peer group that week, someone asks if anyone's had a rough patch lately. What do you do?

options.text: Raise your hand and say what's actually been hard
options.then: Two others nod, and the rough patch feels less like just yours.

options.text: Stay quiet, since it's not that bad compared to others
options.then: You carry it alone, comparing instead of sharing.

options.text: Say everything's been fine to seem like you're coping
options.then: The image holds, but the doubt doesn't actually move.

options.text: Change the subject to something lighter for the group
options.then: The moment for honesty passes without you taking it.

steps.why: Sharing the rough patch with people who understand eases what you're carrying.

steps.prompt: A month later, the doubt returns during a quiet stretch with no news either way. What do you do with it?

options.text: You say it out loud, and tell someone who gets it
options.then: It still stings, but saying it makes room to keep going.

options.text: You assume this time it must really mean something
options.then: The old fear returns full strength, despite everything since.

options.text: You keep it to yourself, since dwelling on it doesn't help
options.then: It sits heavier this time, with nowhere to go.

options.text: You stop the whole process until the doubt fully clears
options.then: The process sits paused for weeks, and the doubt hasn't cleared.

steps.why: Saying the doubt out loud, and not alone, keeps it from stalling you.

scenarios.debrief: Doubt is normal; name it, talk it through with support, and keep going.
scenarios.relearn: Name mid journey doubt and talk it out; it's normal, not a reason to quit.

scenarios.hook: A friend keeps offering the same well-meant, unhelpful advice about your hard route.
scenarios.setup: She brings it up at a wedding function.

steps.prompt: She says: "Just relax. It'll happen when it happens."

options.text: "It's not about relaxing. Steady support is what helps."
options.then: She pauses. "I didn't know that. Tell me more?"

options.text: "Yeah, maybe I'm just overthinking the whole thing."
options.then: She nods, satisfied, and moves on to the next topic.

options.text: "Easy for you to say. You have no idea."
options.then: The music covers an awkward silence between you two.

options.text: "Sure, I'll try."
options.then: She feels helpful, unaware her advice missed the point.

steps.why: Correcting the myth kindly, and naming what helps, protects you from a dismissive line.

steps.prompt: Later, over food, she asks: "Is anything making the waiting easier for you?"

options.text: "A peer group. People who actually get the route."
options.then: She says she never thought of it that way before.

options.text: "Honestly, nothing helps. You just wait it out."
options.then: She hears helplessness, not the real picture.

options.text: "It's complicated. You wouldn't understand."
options.then: She looks a bit hurt and lets the topic drop.

options.text: "I'd rather talk about something else tonight."
options.then: She lets it go, though the myth she started with still stands.

steps.why: Naming real support replaces the vague myth with something specific and true.

steps.prompt: Her mother, sitting nearby, adds: "In our day, nobody overthought these things."

options.text: "Things were different then. This route needs real planning."
options.then: Her mother pauses, then says she hadn't considered that.

options.text: "You're probably right. I should just stop overthinking."
options.then: The old myth gets a second voice backing it now.

options.text: "With respect, that's not really helpful to say."
options.then: The table goes quiet, and the point gets lost in the tone.

options.text: "Sure, whatever you say."
options.then: You let the comment pass, and it settles as if agreed.

steps.why: Naming that this route takes real planning corrects the myth without a clash.

steps.prompt: Weeks later, your friend calls to check in: "So, how are you actually doing with it all?"

options.text: "Up and down. Steady support is what's helping."
options.then: She sounds glad. "Then I'll stop telling people to just relax."

options.text: "Not sure. Maybe I should just relax like you said."
options.then: The old advice creeps back into a conversation that started well.

options.text: "Why does it matter to you now?"
options.then: She backs off, unsure why the question felt sharp.

options.text: "Let's not talk about it. I'm tired of the topic."
options.then: A friend who was genuinely asking gets shut out.

steps.why: Telling her honestly what's helping keeps the talk real and stops the myth coming back.

scenarios.relearn: Kindly correcting 'just relax', even when others repeat it, and naming what helps protects you from a dismissive myth.

scenarios.hook: You and Pooja are months into the wait on your route to family.
scenarios.setup: She brings something up quietly after dinner.

steps.prompt: She says: "The wait feels endless, and I keep doing the money math in my head."

options.text: "Let's actually look at the numbers together this weekend."
options.then: She nods, relieved someone will sit with it instead of just her.

options.text: "Stop worrying so much. It'll sort itself out somehow."
options.then: "That's not actually reassuring," she says, still doing the math.

options.text: "We'll manage. We always do."
options.then: She wants a plan, not a phrase, and the anxiety stays.

options.text: "I'll take on extra work and sort the money myself."
options.then: She frowns. "I don't want you carrying it alone. I want us to plan it."

steps.why: Sitting with the actual numbers together turns worry into a shared plan.

steps.prompt: A few days later, she asks: "What's one realistic thing we can actually aim for?"

options.text: "Setting aside a fixed amount each month for the next step."
options.then: She relaxes a little. "That feels doable."

options.text: "Let's just aim to have the whole thing figured out by next month."
options.then: The target feels too big, and the anxiety creeps back in.

options.text: "I don't know. Whatever happens happens."
options.then: She looks disappointed, having hoped for something concrete.

options.text: "You decide. You're better with numbers anyway."
options.then: The weight lands back on her alone, which is what she was avoiding.

steps.why: A small, concrete savings goal gives the worry somewhere to go without overwhelming you.

steps.prompt: A month later, an unexpected bill sets you back. She asks: "Does this mean we're failing at this?"

options.text: "No. It means we adjust, not that we've failed."
options.then: She exhales. "Okay. Let's work out what to change, then."

options.text: "Maybe we're just bad at planning this stuff."
options.then: The small slip turns into a bigger doubt than it needed to.

options.text: "It's fine. Don't worry about it."
options.then: She wants to talk it through, not have it waved away.

options.text: "You shouldn't have got your hopes up."
options.then: She hears blame, right when she needed steadiness instead.

steps.why: Treating a setback as something to adjust keeps you both steady, not blamed.

scenarios.relearn: Facing the wait and the budget together, with one realistic milestone, beats either panicking or brushing it off.

scenarios.hook: A relative pushes a fast agent who skips the legal steps for your adoption.
scenarios.setup: He brings it up again at Sunday lunch.

steps.prompt: He says: "My friend's agent can get you a child in weeks, no waiting around."

options.text: "Thanks, but we're going through CARA. It's what keeps this safe for us and the child."

options.text: "Okay, maybe I'll just try the agent to save time."

options.text: "That sounds completely illegal, honestly."

steps.prompt: He calls a few days later, saying: "The agent's asking if you're still interested."

options.text: "No. Please let him know we're not interested, clearly."
options.then: "Fine," he says, a little put out, but the calls stop.

options.text: "Tell him maybe. I haven't fully decided."
options.then: The door stays open, and the pressure doesn't let up.

options.text: "Why does he even still have my number?"
options.then: The real question gets lost in an argument about the phone.

options.text: "Just ignore him for now. He'll go away eventually."
options.then: He doesn't go away, and the calls keep coming.

steps.why: A clear, direct no closes the door instead of leaving it slightly open.

steps.prompt: At the next family gathering, the relative tells others: "They're being too cautious about this."

options.text: "We're being lawful, actually. It protects the child too."
options.then: A cousin nods, saying she'd never thought of it that way.

options.text: "Maybe he's right. We are being a bit much."
options.then: The doubt creeps in, right as the relative repeats his claim to others.

options.text: "Stop talking about our family business to everyone."
options.then: The room tenses, and the actual point gets lost.

options.text: "Let him say what he wants."
options.then: The misinformation stands uncorrected in front of the family.

steps.why: Naming the lawful route as protection, not caution, corrects the misinformation calmly.

scenarios.relearn: Declining a fast agent and naming the lawful route protects you and the child from a real risk.

scenarios.hook: At a peer group, you want to admit how heavy the wait feels instead of pretending you're fine.

options.text: "I'm totally fine, no problems at all here."
options.then: The room moves on, and the weight stays quietly with you.

options.text: "Everything's fine, though this whole process is unfair."
options.then: The anger lands, but the actual heaviness underneath stays unsaid.

options.text: "I'd rather listen to others today."
options.then: You hear their stories, but yours goes unspoken again.

steps.prompt: Someone across the circle says: "The waiting's been heavy for me this month. How do you all get through it?"

options.text: "Honestly, it's heavy for me too. Coming here helps."
options.then: She smiles. "That's exactly why I keep coming back too."

options.text: "Nothing really helps. I just push through it somehow."

options.text: "I don't know yet. Ask me next month."
options.then: The question sits unanswered, and so does the support.

options.text: "I'd rather not get into mine today."
options.then: That's respected, though the moment for support passes.

steps.why: Admitting the weight, and what helps, lets the group hold it with you.

steps.prompt: After the session, one member asks quietly: "Do you want to talk, just the two of us?"

options.text: "Yes, I'd really like that. Thank you for asking."
options.then: You end up talking for an hour, and it genuinely helps.

options.text: "I think I've said enough for one day."
options.then: She nods, and the offer quietly closes for now.

options.text: "Maybe, if you've been waiting longer than me."

options.text: "Sure, but let's talk about something lighter."

steps.prompt: A month later, a newer member admits, for the first time: "This waiting feels so heavy some days."

options.text: "Thank you for saying that. I've felt that too."
options.then: She relaxes visibly, hearing she's not the only one.

options.text: "You'll get used to it. Everyone does eventually."
options.then: It's meant kindly, but it brushes past what she just admitted.

options.text: "Wait until you're further along. It gets heavier."
options.then: Her face falls, and the room feels a little tenser.

options.text: "Try not to focus on the hard parts too much."
options.then: She hears that her feeling wasn't quite the right one to share.

steps.why: Meeting her honesty with your own keeps the group a place people can admit the truth.

scenarios.relearn: Naming how heavy the wait feels, out loud and with peers, shares the weight instead of carrying it alone.

scenarios.hook: A clinic gives you sobering odds and you feel the urge to dismiss them.
scenarios.setup: The doctor waits for your reaction after explaining.

steps.prompt: She asks: "Do you have any questions about what these odds mean for you?"

options.text: "Thank you for being straight with me. Can we talk it through?"

options.text: "Can you just tell me it'll definitely, absolutely work, so I feel better?"

options.text: "I'd rather not go through what they mean right now."
options.then: You leave with numbers you haven't really taken in.

options.text: "These odds sound wrong. Can you check again?"
options.then: She confirms them kindly, and nothing about them changes.

steps.why: Welcoming the honest odds lets you plan around what's real, not a false promise.

steps.prompt: Your partner asks afterward: "What did you actually take away from the appointment?"

options.text: "That we should plan for more than one attempt, honestly."
options.then: He nods. "Okay. Let's build that into the plan, then."

options.text: "That it'll probably be fine either way."
options.then: He hears reassurance instead of the plan you'll actually need.

options.text: "That the clinic might just be too cautious."
options.then: "Maybe," he says, "but what do we actually do with that?"

options.text: "I don't really want to talk about it yet."
options.then: The odds sit unprocessed between the two of you.

steps.why: Sharing the honest odds with your partner turns them into a plan you both hold.

steps.prompt: A friend, hearing the odds, says: "That sounds discouraging. Maybe find a clinic that's more positive."

options.text: "Honest odds aren't discouraging. They're what I actually trust."
options.then: She pauses. "I hadn't thought of it that way before."

options.text: "Maybe you're right. I'll look around."
options.then: You start chasing a more comfortable answer, not a true one.

options.text: "It is discouraging, and I really don't want to talk about it anymore."
options.then: The conversation ends before the honest odds get their due.

steps.why: Naming that real acceptance can't be priced at hiding yourself keeps your integrity intact.

options.text: Wonder if you're the reason the family is so tense

scenarios.debrief: Community support lightens what solo parenting can make heavy alone.

scenarios.hook: At a family lunch, an uncle says your adopted daughter will 'never really be one of us'.

options.text: Say firmly she is fully your daughter and family

options.then: It lets the slight land on her, unanswered.

options.text: Say you'll speak to him about it privately, later
options.then: It postpones the moment your daughter needed answered right then.

options.text: Pull her aside quietly instead of answering him
options.then: It protects the moment, but leaves his comment standing unanswered.

steps.why: Naming your daughter as fully yours draws the line and shows her you stand for her.

steps.prompt: Later, your daughter asks if what he said was true. What do you tell her?

options.text: Say plainly that it isn't, and never will be
options.then: She holds onto that, visibly steadier than before.

options.text: Say some people just don't understand families like ours
options.then: It explains him, but doesn't quite answer her actual question.

options.text: Say not to worry about what he thinks
options.then: It skips past whether it's true, which is what she actually asked.

options.text: Say you'll talk to him about it later
options.then: She's left with the question still open in the meantime.

steps.why: A plain, direct answer settles her question instead of just managing his behaviour.

steps.prompt: At the next family gathering, the uncle avoids the topic entirely. What do you do?

options.text: Keep her close, and include her in everything as family
options.then: She stays at your side, relaxed, part of every conversation.

options.text: Act as if nothing ever happened, to keep things easy

steps.why: Including her fully, in front of everyone, keeps showing her she belongs, whatever was said before.

steps.prompt: A cousin later asks quietly if the uncle's comment still bothers your daughter. What do you say?

options.text: Say you're not sure, and you'll gently ask her

options.text: Say kids forget things like that quickly
options.then: It assumes something you haven't actually checked.

options.text: Say you'd rather not bring it up again with her
options.then: Avoiding the check-in leaves a small question mark hanging.

options.text: Say it's not something to dwell on
options.then: It closes a conversation that might have been worth having with her.

steps.why: Admitting you don't know, and asking her gently, puts her feelings ahead of guesses.

scenarios.debrief: Name your child as fully yours; don't trade her dignity for an easy lunch.

scenarios.hook: You're proud of your family but feel pressure to post a 'normal' version of it online.

steps.prompt: Months later, someone in your family wants to post photos of you all. What do you say?

options.text: Say yes, and pick the photos together, proudly

options.text: Say yes, but keep it low-key so nobody asks questions

scenarios.debrief: Show your family as it really is when you choose to share. Keeping things private is your call. Editing yourself under pressure is the trap.

options.text: Explain that they show up the way family does

scenarios.hook: Your teen child asks if they should hide the family's shape from a new friend.

options.text: Say to hide it for now, just to be safe

scenarios.debrief: Teach pride plus the right to choose whom to trust, not shame or hiding.

scenarios.hook: You overhear your child apologising to a friend for having 'no dad'.

scenarios.hook: A colleague at lunch keeps glancing at you with quiet pity.
scenarios.setup: You want a settled reply, not a defensive one.

steps.prompt: She says: "So it's just you and no kids? That's... sad."

options.text: "It's a full, good life, and it suits me."
options.then: She blinks. "Oh. I didn't think of it that way."

options.text: "Yeah... maybe someday. Who knows."
options.then: It leaves the pity standing, unanswered.

options.text: "Why would you assume that's sad?"
options.then: She flushes. "I didn't mean it like that."

options.text: "That's really none of your business, is it?"
options.then: She stiffens. "I only meant it kindly." A pause, then she tries again.

steps.why: Naming your life as full and settled answers the pity without needing to defend it.

steps.prompt: She asks: "But don't you ever get lonely?"

options.text: "Sometimes, like anyone, but my life is full."
options.then: She nods, a little more thoughtful now.

options.text: "Never, not even once."
options.then: It sounds a little too tidy to actually be believed.

options.text: "That's a strange question to ask."
options.then: She shrugs. "Fair. Maybe it was too personal."

options.text: "I have my friends and family, so it's fine."
options.then: It answers around the question rather than meeting it directly.

steps.why: Answering honestly, without over-explaining, keeps the reply settled and believable.

steps.prompt: She says: "I just always assumed you'd want a family eventually."

options.text: "I do have one. It just looks different from yours."
options.then: She pauses. "I hadn't thought of it like that."

options.text: "Everyone assumes that. It's fine."
options.then: She nods, unsure if that was really an answer.

options.text: "Maybe you shouldn't assume things about people."
options.then: She winces. "Okay, noted, I guess."

options.text: "I used to think that too, honestly."
options.then: She nods, taking it as something close to agreement.

steps.why: Naming your own family, in your own terms, corrects the assumption without a lecture.

steps.prompt: Later, a mutual colleague asks: "I heard you're not planning on kids. Is that true?"

options.text: "True. My life's full, and it suits me."
options.then: The colleague smiles. "That's lovely to hear."

options.text: "Did she say that? What else did she say?"
